title: Stacks, expressions and recursion
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 2
subtitle: Last in, first out — and why that is exactly the shape of function calls.

sections.title: The stack ADT
sections.body: A stack allows insertion and removal only at one end, the top: push adds, pop removes, peek reads. The last item pushed is the first popped (LIFO). An array with a top index implements it; overflow (push on full) and underflow (pop on empty) must be checked. All operations are O(1).

questions.prompt: Push 1, 2, 3 then pop twice. What is on top?

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — The stack ADT

sections.title: Infix to postfix with a stack
sections.body: Humans write infix (A+B) which needs precedence rules; postfix (AB+) does not. To convert: operands go straight to the output; an operator first pops any stacked operator of higher or equal precedence, then is pushed; "(" is pushed, ")" pops until "(". At the end pop everything. A+B*C−(D/E) becomes A B C * + D E / -.

worked.why: Evaluate the postfix of (2+3)*4−6/2 using a stack of numbers: push operands, each operator pops two.

questions.prompt: In A+B*C, which operator is applied first, and what does the postfix look like?

choices.text: Left to right; A B + C *.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: * has higher precedence, so B and C are multiplied before the addition.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — infix → postfix
figures.note: Stack on the bottom row, output above it.

sections.title: Recursion
sections.body: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller one. It needs a base case (stop) and a step that moves toward it. Each call gets its own frame on the call stack; returns unwind it. Factorial: n! = n × (n−1)!, with 0! = 1. Run it and the Lab shows the stack grow and shrink.

questions.prompt: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

choices.text: It recurses until the stack overflows.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every call makes another call; frames pile up without end.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.1 — Recursion
figures.note: fact(5) makes 5 nested calls, then multiplies on the way back.

sections.title: Tower of Hanoi
sections.body: Move n disks from A to C using B, one at a time, never a larger on a smaller. Recursively: move n−1 disks A→B, move the largest A→C, move n−1 disks B→C. The count satisfies T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1, so T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1. For 4 disks: 15 moves.

sections.title: Recursion versus iteration
sections.body: Anything recursive can be written with a loop and an explicit stack. Recursion is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; it costs stack space and call overhead. Tail recursion (the recursive call is the last action) can be turned into a loop by the compiler. Naive Fibonacci recurses twice and recomputes the same values exponentially — memoisation fixes it.

questions.prompt: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci slow?

choices.text: It recomputes the same sub-problems exponentially many times.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: fib(n) calls fib(n−1) and fib(n−2), which overlap heavily.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Stack = LIFO, O(1) push/pop; it underlies calls, undo and expression evaluation.
  • Recursion = base case + smaller problem; the call stack holds the frames.
